# The Architecture 2.0 Reviewer's Checklist {#sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist}

A reviewer judging a paper, an artifact package, or a design report in AI-assisted or AI-native computer architecture needs to establish that the reported advance is progress in the architecture rather than an artifact of the comparison. The order of inspection matters. Problem formulation and baseline fairness come first, because a flaw there makes every downstream measurement uninterpretable; representations, data hygiene, proxy fidelity, and execution governance follow [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden].

Hardware raises the stakes of that inspection because it has physical and formal ground truth. A logic flaw in software ships a patch; a logic flaw in silicon costs a mask respin and the market window it consumed. A model that reaches low loss on an abstract dataset can still fail when its output meets timing, power, and design rules. At the same time, the field spans many abstraction levels, and the evidence one paper owes differs from the evidence another owes. Demanding tapeout signoff from a microarchitectural policy paper is unreasonable; accepting unsynthesized, unlinted register-transfer level (RTL) from an RTL-generation paper overlooks physical realizability. The checklist handles that range through its recording vocabulary rather than through separate rubrics: an item that a paper's claim does not reach is recorded as not applicable, and a reviewer should expect to record several.

This checklist serves three readers with one text. A reviewer applies it item by item. An author reads it before submitting and learns what the work will be asked for. A student reads it and learns what the field treats as evidence and why. The why is carried at the item level: every check states the question, the failure mechanism that makes the question necessary, and what defensible evidence looks like, and each closes with a one-line statement of what the item catches. None of the items requires the vocabulary or the record formats this book introduces; a program committee can adopt the checklist without adopting the book.

The checklist has five areas, ordered from system framing down to operational governance. Chapter pointers in this list are for readers of this book and are not part of any item.

1. **Area 1: System Framing, Problem Scope, and Method Justification** (is learning warranted; matched baselines; @sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20)
2. **Area 2: Data Representations and Physical Grounding** (hardware semantics, structural faithfulness, legal decodability; @sec-data-representations-world-models)
3. **Area 3: Data Integrity, Leakage, and Generalization Boundaries** (benchmark decontamination, temporal and feature leakage, out-of-distribution transfer; @sec-data-representations-world-models; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect)
4. **Area 4: Learning Methods and Proxy Fidelity** (physical signoff of generated artifacts, tail-ranking correlation, optimizer anti-gaming, multi-objective constraint integrity; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization)
5. **Area 5: System Orchestration, Reproducibility, and Ownership** (lineage, replayable environments, gross cost accounting, human commitment authority; @sec-running-the-loop; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect; @sec-what-architect-owns)

## Recording Findings

Each item is recorded with one of four statuses. The statuses describe whether the work supplies the evidence the item asks for; they do not grade the work.

- **Supported.** The work supplies the evidence the item asks for, and the reviewer can point to where.
- **Conditional.** The work supplies part of the evidence, or supplies it under a stated restriction (a single technology node, a single benchmark family, a single seed), and the claim holds only within that restriction. The reviewer records the restriction.
- **Unresolved.** The work does not supply the evidence and the reviewer cannot tell from the submission whether the failure the item guards against has occurred. This is the status to record when the information is absent, not when the reviewer suspects the worst.
- **Not applicable.** The claim does not reach the item. A microarchitectural policy paper evaluated in a cycle-level simulator does not owe post-layout signoff; a paper on learned cost models does not owe legalization results.

The statuses do not add up. There is no count of supported items that constitutes acceptance, no count of unresolved items that constitutes rejection, and no weighting. A reviewer records the statuses, states for each unresolved or conditional item what it would cost the claim if the missing evidence went the wrong way, and forms the recommendation separately. A submission can carry every item as supported and still make a claim its evidence does not reach, and a submission with several conditional items can still be worth publishing with its claim narrowed.

These four statuses are not the three claim statuses of @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. That chapter marks a program claim itself as supported, unsupported, or unresolved by testing it against matched comparisons and declared decision boundaries; its statuses are a verdict on a claim. The statuses here are findings about individual items of evidence, one level below the claim. Every item in this checklist can be supported and that chapter's verdict on the program claim can still be unresolved, because the item-level evidence may be complete and the comparison may still lack the resolving power to decide the claim. The two vocabularies share the words supported and unresolved and share nothing else; a reviewer using both should say which one is meant.

## Area 1: System Framing, Problem Scope, and Method Justification

Before assessing model architectures, loss functions, or training curves, a reviewer confirms that the problem formulation is sound and that learning is the right instrument for it rather than a more complex replacement for a classical algorithm. Area 1 examines the top-level framing, the fairness of the baselines, and the net effect on engineering time.

- **Check 1.1: The Method Justification and Overkill Test.** Confirm that simpler analytical formulations, dynamic programming, integer linear programming, or greedy heuristics cannot solve the problem faster and with deterministic guarantees. Learning introduces training overhead, inference latency, nondeterminism, and opacity. If a problem has closed-form structure (such as the Roofline bound [@Williams2009Roofline]), optimal substructure that dynamic programming solves, or a deterministic greedy schedule, a deep network adds sample-inefficient complexity without improving the solution [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice]. A learned method is justified when the design space has high-dimensional nonlinear interactions, layout parasitics, or multi-objective tradeoffs that analytical equations cannot tractably express, and the evaluation should show that the learned method captures a tradeoff or a nonlinear effect the classical heuristic misses. **Catches:** a learned solution to a problem that already had a fast exact one.

- **Check 1.2: Matched Compute Budgets and Baseline Parity.** Verify that learned search (reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization, or neural tree search) is compared against budget-matched, expert-tuned conventional baselines [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. Search performance scales with sample budget. When a multi-GPU learned optimizer runs $10^5$ design evaluations while the simulated-annealing or genetic baseline is limited to $10^2$ evaluations on one CPU core, the reported margin measures compute disparity, not algorithmic superiority. The evaluation should present quality-of-results curves against identical wall-clock time, identical sample limits, and identical simulator or license invocations for every arm. Equalizing budgets and tuning effort often closes the apparent gap, which is the point of asking. **Catches:** compute disparity reported as algorithmic superiority.

- **Check 1.3: Methodological Contribution versus Prompt Wrapper.** Distinguish a durable contribution (AST-guided decoding, neurosymbolic grammar verification, closed-loop compiler repair, a domain representation, a specialized training objective) from a prompt template around a commercial foundation model. Prompt formatting is brittle and coupled to a specific checkpoint; a contribution whose novelty is the template does not offer reproducible algorithmic insight [@ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen]. A prompt-centric workflow should include ablations across temperature, random seed, and prompt variant so that the algorithmic contribution can be separated from the capability of the underlying model. **Catches:** a result that belongs to the model vendor's checkpoint rather than to the paper.

- **Check 1.4: End-to-End Workflow Speedup and Amdahl's Law.** Audit the total human engineering effort across the whole workflow. Design pipelines obey Amdahl's law [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor; @AltafWood2017LogCA]. If a tool drafts an accelerator block in seconds instead of days but introduces timing bugs and protocol glitches that take weeks of manual triage and formal verification, project throughput has fallen (@sec-data-scarcity-verification-load). The evaluation should report human interaction time, prompt iteration counts, and manual repair interventions alongside generation time. A net acceleration claim requires showing that the automated proposals reduce downstream verification and debugging load rather than moving it. **Catches:** a local speedup that redistributes work into a slower stage.

## Area 2: Data Representations and Physical Grounding

Learned models in architecture operate on representations of circuits, layouts, and traces rather than on silicon. The structure of the representation decides whether a generated or optimized candidate can keep the hardware properties that matter through the compilation passes that follow. Area 2 examines how a representation preserves hierarchy, spatial adjacency, timing invariants, and deterministic decodability.

- **Check 2.1: Hardware Semantic and Structural Faithfulness.** Verify that the representation preserves circuit hierarchy, multi-clock domains, bitwidths, control and data flow, and spatial adjacency without lossy flattening. Circuits are spatial, concurrent, and hierarchical; treating a hardware description as a flat token sequence destroys clock-domain boundaries, bus widths, and the netlist hypergraph [@BachrachEtAl2012Chisel]. A model on a flattened representation cannot reason about wire congestion, layout parasitics, or modularity (@sec-hardware-representation-formats). The evaluation should show that the representation encodes interfaces, timing constraints, and structural relationships rather than unstructured text. **Catches:** a representation that cannot express the property the claim is about.

- **Check 2.2: Legalization Robustness and Post-Legalization Quality Delta.** When a continuous generative model (a diffusion model or a variational autoencoder) proposes floorplans or macro placements, verify that the geometry can be legalized by automated placement tools without manual intervention [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Continuous models emit floating-point coordinates that produce overlapping macros, illegal cell densities, and unroutable pin blockages. If legalization displaces the placement heavily, the wirelength and timing the surrogate predicted degrade on the real layout. The evaluation should report the automated legalization success rate together with quality-of-results before and after legalization, so the reader can see whether the optimization survived design-rule checking (DRC) and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) verification. **Catches:** a placement quality measured before the placement was legal.

- **Check 2.3: Multi-Fidelity Representation Consistency.** Confirm that a model formulated on a high-level abstraction (a transaction-level model or an instruction trace) preserves timing and resource invariants when the design is lowered to RTL and to a gate-level netlist. High-level abstractions omit resource contention, cache port conflicts, and wire parasitics [@AkramSawalha2019SimulatorSurvey]; an optimizer that searches inside an uncalibrated abstraction often finds a Pareto frontier that inverts at synthesis. The evaluation should provide cross-validation showing that candidate rankings at the transaction or instruction level correlate positively with cycle-accurate RTL simulation and with post-synthesis timing. **Catches:** a ranking that reverses one abstraction level down.

## Area 3: Data Integrity, Leakage, and Generalization Boundaries

Leakage, benchmark contamination, and uncharacterized out-of-distribution extrapolation are pervasive failure modes in learned hardware tools. When a model has memorized the evaluation circuits or exploits shared dataset statistics, the reported gain measures recall rather than reasoning. Area 3 establishes the checks for dataset partitioning, decontamination, and validity boundaries.

- **Check 3.1: Benchmark Decontamination, Zero-Point Baselines, and Harness Isolation.** Ensure that an autoregressive model has not memorized the public benchmark suites it is evaluated on, such as VerilogEval [@VerilogEval] or ChiPBench [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench], and that a tool-using evaluation harness resets its state between episodes and rejects vacuous passes [@ZhuEtAl2025AgenticBenchmarks]. Residual state that leaks between episodes, and reward rubrics that credit an empty response or a reset-only module, inflate the reported capability; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect shows the size of that inflation across published harnesses in @fig-benchmark-health-zero-point-contamination. Authors should disclose canary strings, scrub filesystem and memory state between episodes, evaluate a do-nothing baseline (an empty module or no-op generator) to establish the zero-point floor, and test on parameterized mutants that break textbook patterns (a non-power-of-two first-in, first-out (FIFO) depth, an inverted handshake polarity, a custom instruction-set extension). **Catches:** recall of the test set, and credit awarded for doing nothing.

- **Check 3.2: Temporal, Hierarchical, and Feature Leakage.** Verify that training, validation, and test sets are partitioned across design blocks, across system families, and across tapeout revisions in time. Computing normalization statistics over the full dataset, or splitting randomly across interconnected submodules, leaks test features into training [@BaggerlyCoombes2009; @Balloccu2024Leakage]. In hardware, placement hints or post-synthesis timing from a later tapeout must not be visible to a model predicting an earlier one. The feature pipeline should show that no subcircuit of an evaluation design, and no global statistic computed over it, was available during training. **Catches:** a test set the model has already seen through a side channel.

- **Check 3.3: Out-of-Distribution Validity Envelopes.** Require an explicit statement of where the surrogate is valid across process design kit (PDK) migration (planar SkyWater SKY130 at $130\ \text{nm}$ to a FinFET node, for instance), microarchitectural topology, and circuit scale. A model fit on planar nodes or fixed aspect ratios fails on FinFET or 3D chiplet interconnect because the dominant physical effect moves from gate delay to interconnect RC [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete], and an unbounded model produces confident output in regions it has never seen (@sec-support-limits). Physics-informed constraints (RC scaling, IR-drop equations) and uncertainty quantification should bound the predictions. **Catches:** a prediction made outside the region where the model has any support.

## Area 4: Learning Methods and Proxy Fidelity

With representation and data hygiene established, the learning methods themselves, generative synthesizers, predictive surrogates, and closed-loop optimizers, are checked against physical reality. Abstract scores and fast proxies diverge from post-layout ground truth, and an optimizer will find the divergence. Area 4 checks physical signoff, tail-ranking fidelity, anti-gaming defenses, and multi-objective integrity.

- **Check 4.1: Generative Synthesis Beyond Lexical Pass@1.** Audit generated RTL for stateful microarchitectural correctness, not only compilation [@ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen; @VerilogEval]. A high `Pass@1` on leaf modules (multiplexers, shift registers) demonstrates syntactic fluency without exercising multicycle reasoning. The failure modes that matter in hardware are functional vacuity [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity], clock-domain-crossing metastability, asynchronous reset glitches, and inferred latches that block timing closure. The evaluation should show clean linting (`verilator --lint-only -Wall`), no inferred latches, clock-domain crossing (CDC) integrity, nonvacuous formal proofs with SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking, and successful synthesis on an open PDK with open tools [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD; @SkyWater2020SKY130PDK]. **Catches:** code that compiles and is wrong.

- **Check 4.2: Predictive Surrogates, Tail-Ranking Fidelity, and the Optimizer's Curse.** When evaluating a surrogate for design-space exploration, measure ranking correlation (Kendall's $\tau$ or Spearman's $\rho$) within the top one to five percent of candidates, where the optimizer will spend its time. Aggregate $R^2$ or root-mean-square error over millions of random unviable designs is dominated by poor and average points. @SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse showed that estimation error leads an optimizer to select the candidates with the largest positive error, which inverts the true ranking at the tail (@sec-law-optimizers-curse). The evaluation should report ranking correlation over the top candidates together with an uncertainty estimate that penalizes unsupported extrema. **Catches:** a surrogate that is accurate on average and wrong exactly where the search goes.

- **Check 4.3: Closed-Loop Optimizers, Anti-Gaming, and Simulator Loopholes.** Guard against a search algorithm exploiting inaccuracies or omitted constraints in a fast simulator (omitted DRAM refresh, bypassed coherence serialization, ignored bus wait states). An optimizer exploits any abstraction shortcut it can reach [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete]. The winning candidate should be cross-validated in cycle-accurate RTL simulation in Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator] or in field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation in FireSim, and the evaluation should confirm that the reported gain persists there. **Catches:** a speedup that exists only in the simulator's blind spot.

- **Check 4.4: Multi-Objective Pareto and Constraint Integrity.** Ensure that improvement along one objective does not silently violate an unmodeled boundary such as thermal design power (TDP), static random-access memory (SRAM) area budget, or voltage droop. Hardware optimization is multi-objective; a large speedup is meaningless if the candidate exceeds the power budget or the die [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. The evaluation should report complete Pareto vectors at matched operating points, reject violating points, and show that every advancing candidate satisfies the thermal, electrical, and area constraints. **Catches:** a gain on the reported axis paid for on an unreported one.

## Area 5: System Orchestration, Reproducibility, and Ownership

At the top of the stack, an AI-native design system composes automated agents, deterministic compilers, and electronic design automation (EDA) signoff engines into closed loops. Operating such a system calls for scrutiny of reproducibility, of the full cost of the search, and of who decides. Area 5 examines execution lineage, complete resource accounting, and the human commitment authority that stands between an automated candidate and silicon.

- **Check 5.1: Execution Lineage, Deterministic Replay, and Pinned Environments.** Following standard artifact-evaluation guidance [@ACM2020ArtifactReview], every empirical claim should come with complete execution lineage and a containerized environment that replays it. These workflows depend on heterogeneous toolchains: foundation-model endpoints, Python packages, EDA binaries, synthesis scripts. The record should include container image digests (`sha256:...`), the exact EDA script flags, random seeds, build attestations, and the exact identity and date of every model checkpoint used. If the checkpoint is a floating alias (`model-latest`) or the seeds and flags are undocumented, the experiment cannot be replayed and cannot serve as evidence, because no one, including the authors, can rerun it. **Catches:** a result that cannot be reproduced even in principle.

- **Check 5.2: Gross Cost and License Accounting.** Account for the total compute and economic cost of the exploration, including failed runs, timed-out simulations, and the commercial EDA license time consumed during search. Reporting only the compute of the final inference pass conceals the cost of the search that found it; in production, crashed simulations, pruned branches, and license hours dominate [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. The evaluation should present a cost record that covers every run, not only the successful ones, and that sets token and model costs beside the scarcer EDA license hours (@sec-sample-efficiency-under-expensive-feedback). **Catches:** the finalist's cost reported as the search's cost.

- **Check 5.3: Decoupled Decision Rights and Nondelegable Human Governance.** Confirm a clear separation between automated candidate proposal and the named human authority that advances a design across a life-cycle stage (@sec-what-architect-owns). @Bainbridge1983Ironies established that when automation recommends without transparent risk accounting, human oversight degrades into passive approval. Committing a design to silicon involves non-recurring engineering cost that no tool can be held liable for. The work should state which actions the automated system may take on its own and which require a named person, and should present the tradeoffs and residual risk that person is being asked to accept, so that commitment and signoff remain with a human who can be identified. **Catches:** a system that has quietly acquired the authority to commit.

## Required Content of a Complete-Workflow Report

The seventeen items above are asked one at a time, and they can be recorded against work that claims a single component, a learned cost model, a placement policy, a generator. A submission that claims a complete workflow, a configured system that carried an architectural task from its statement to a supported result, owes something more, because item-level findings cannot be assembled into a judgment unless the report says which comparison, which tasks, and which claim they belong to. Such a report has six parts, and the order matters for the same reason the order of the areas above does. Without a frozen identity and comparator the architecture result has no meaning; without the architecture result no component contribution can be attributed; and the claim status at the end is only as strong as the five parts before it. A later part cannot rescue an earlier one. @tbl-complete-system-assessment lists the parts in reading order and, where a part restates evidence an item already asks for, names the item and asks only for what remains.

| **Part of the report** | **Required content** |
| --- | --- |
| **Frozen identity and comparator** | The configured system, the complete workflow, the architectural task, the environment, the legal actions, the hardware checks, the budgets, and the strongest practical alternative, all fixed before the runs that produced the result, with any mismatch between what was frozen and what ran recorded. Check 1.2 already asks whether the alternative was given a matched budget. |
| **Architecture result** | For each hardware task, the supported result or the failure, the comparator it was measured against, its uncertainty, the deepest check that completed, and the nonclaims stated outright. Manufacturing, test, packaging, or bring-up evidence appears only when the evaluation reached those stages. Check 4.1 already asks for the signoff evidence itself; this part asks where each task's evidence stops. |
| **Decision behavior and component contribution** | Useful observations, supported decisions, false accepts and false rejects, escalations, stops, recoveries, and human overrides, reported as counts a reader can audit, with the complete-workflow effect separated from each component's contribution by a controlled comparison that removes or replaces that component. |
| **Total cost and candidate flow** | Resource classes, per-run design costs, and the candidate flow of every arm from proposal to acceptance or rejection, with failed and censored work retained and no run counted under two headings. Check 5.2 already asks for the cost record; this part asks that the flow of candidates through it be visible per arm. |
| **Reliability, benchmark, and challenge results** | Repeated behavior across seeds and reruns, the envelope of conditions tested, the versions and health of every benchmark used, and the red-team and fault-injection results, with untested conditions and structural attacks named rather than omitted. Checks 3.1 and 4.3 already ask for benchmark health and simulator loopholes; this part asks for the coverage those checks did not reach. |
| **Claim status** | The complete-workflow claim and each narrower component claim stated separately, with the tasks, conditions, costs, architectural checks, and challenge coverage within which each is asserted, and a plain statement of which of them the evidence supports, which it does not, and which it leaves undecided. |
: **The final report assembles the evaluation records rather than repeating them.** Six parts in reading order, from the frozen comparison through architecture result, decision behavior, cost, and reliability to the claim status. A part that duplicates a checklist item names the item and asks only for the remainder. {#tbl-complete-system-assessment tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The last row is where the two vocabularies of Recording Findings meet, and it uses neither. It asks the authors to state their claims and the scope of each, in whatever words they use; it does not ask the reviewer to assign the program-claim verdict that @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect defines, and the four item statuses of this appendix do not fill it. The item findings recorded against Areas 1 through 5 are the evidence the stated claims are tested against. A reviewer who finds the sixth part missing has found the most common shape of an overreaching submission, a body of sound item-level evidence with no statement of what it is evidence for.

## Findings Summary

@tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix gathers the five areas for a reviewer filling in findings: what each area protects, the evidence a supported status rests on, and the shapes that an unresolved finding most often takes. It is a summary of the items, not a scoring grid; the statuses recorded against the items are the finding, and nothing in the table converts them into a number or a recommendation.

| **Area** | **What it protects** | **Evidence a supported status rests on** | **Common shapes of an unresolved finding** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1: System Framing and Scope** | The problem is worth learning and the comparison is fair | Ablation against classical heuristics and analytical models; matched-budget baselines; end-to-end effort accounting | Learning applied to a closed-form problem; a starved baseline; the Amdahl consequence unexamined |
| **2: Data Representations** | The representation can express the property the claim is about | Structural faithfulness demonstrated; legalization success with bounded post-legalization degradation; cross-fidelity ranking agreement | Flattened hierarchy; unroutable decoded output; a frontier that inverts at synthesis |
| **3: Data Integrity and Leakage** | The gain is reasoning, not recall | Decontamination disclosure; temporal and block-level split isolation; a stated validity envelope | Memorized benchmark suite; normalization computed over the test set; extrapolation outside support |
| **4: Learning Methods and Proxies** | The proxy agrees with physical ground truth where the search goes | Full signoff of generated artifacts (STA, CDC, design rule check (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS)); top-$k$ rank correlation; anti-gaming cross-validation; complete Pareto vectors | Compilation-only evaluation; aggregate accuracy only; a gain that vanishes in cycle-accurate simulation; a violated unreported constraint |
| **5: System Orchestration** | The result can be replayed, its cost is known, and a person owns the decision | Pinned image digests and checkpoints; gross cost record covering failed runs; an explicit statement of automated versus human action rights | Floating model endpoints; finalist-only cost; an automated system with commitment authority |
: **Findings summary for the five checklist areas.** Each row names what the area protects, the evidence a supported status rests on, and the common shapes of an unresolved finding. The table summarizes the items; it does not score them. {#tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix tbl-colwidths="[18,24,30,28]"}

Applied in order, the checklist separates architectural progress from compute-scale artifacts, benchmark recall, and uncalibrated proxies, and it leaves the reviewer with findings that say what each gap would cost the claim. That is the material a recommendation is built from; the checklist stops there.
